entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The British Orthodox Church (BOC) is a small autocephalous Oriental Orthodox Christian denomination in the United Kingdom under the Coptic Pope of Alexandria — established to provide a home for British Christians drawn to Oriental Orthodox (Coptic) Christianity without requiring them to integrate into the primarily Egyptian Coptic church. The BOC attempts to express Orthodox Christianity through traditional British liturgical and theological heritage while maintaining communion with the Coptic Orthodox Church.

The British Orthodox Church represents one of several Western Christian attempts to adopt Eastern Orthodox theology and spirituality in a culturally indigenous Western form — a recurring impulse in 20th-century ecumenical history. The founding figures included John Kersey and other Britons who were drawn to the Coptic Orthodox tradition and worked to establish an officially recognized autocephalous church for British Orthodox Christians.

The BOC's relationship with the Coptic Orthodox Church gives it unusual legitimacy among non-Eastern Orthodox churches seeking Eastern connections: the Coptic Orthodox Church (one of the world's oldest Christian churches, tracing to the apostle Mark in Alexandria, 1st century CE) is fully independent of Rome and Constantinople and has the authority to grant communion and recognition to affiliated churches. The BOC's tiny size (a few hundred to a few thousand members) contrasts with its theological ambition of representing a genuine indigenous British form of Orthodox Christianity.
